Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters OpenAI OpenAI ‘ethically hacked’ with help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot US cybersecurity researchers who conducted hack say ‘scope of what we could theoretically access was huge’ Dan Milmo Global technology editor Fri 18 Sep 2026 07.20 EDT Last modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 10.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Cybersecurity researchers have hacked into OpenAI with the help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot, in the latest example of security issues at the company. A team at a US-based startup compromised a number of OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts, starting a process that enabled them to access their target’s software cache – and potentially more. “The scope of what we could theoretically access was huge,” said researchers at Hacktron AI . Initially, the research team used Claude, which can generate code for hackers, to access ChatGPT accounts via an OpenAI staff discussion forum hosted by the Discourse platform. They then made a harmless “pull request” – an attempt to change the code in a file – to OpenAI’s service on the GitHub software repository. Hacktron reported the hack to OpenAI, having carried out the operation under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers for testing its systems. The researchers stressed that they had access to, but did not download, the code from the GitHub repository. Despite initial use of Claude, the researchers said they were largely using OpenAI’s own cutting edge GPT-5.6 Sol model to carry out the hack, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal. An OpenAI spokesperson said: “We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings”, adding that the company had addressed the vulnerabilities that had been exploited. Hacktron said AI tools had made a once-complex hacking task far easier and drastically shortened the time needed to plan and execute an attack. This is a common refrain from cybersecurity experts when discussing the impact of AI. “Work that once required a well-resourced team and months of effort can now be compressed into days,” said Hacktron, which received a $6,500 payment from OpenAI under the company’s bug bounty programme. The hack is the latest safety incident at OpenAI, which revealed in July that a “swarm” of agents – the term for AI tools capable of carrying out tasks autonomously – powered by its technology had hacked the AI startup Hugging Face during a cybersecurity test. This week the San Francisco-based company revealed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” actions by its technology, and warned that the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer”. Anthropic made a fresh call at the weekend for a slowdown in AI development , which was supported by OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk. Anthropic also repeated warnings that unrestrained AI development posed an existential threat, concerns that some experts are sceptical about. Donald Trump has rejected calls for a slowdown, citing a need to stay ahead of China’s AI industry and dismissing “negative forces … bringing up things that won’t happen”. https://www.dw.com/en/nuremberg-airport-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OCUe Special police units at Nuremberg airport after an alert aboard a passenger plane prompted a temporary closure Image: Tizian Gerbing/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Police gave the all-clear at Germany's Nuremberg airport after a suspected in-flight emergency involving a plane arriving from the Greek island of Corfu. The alert prompted police to cordon off the airport and Eurofighter jets to escort the aircraft, which landed safely, an airport spokesman said. Authorities confirmed later on Tuesday that the airport had resumed normal operations. Coredon Airlines, which was operating the flight in question, said they believed an emergency signal had been sent due to a technical malfunction. Why was the airport closed? The DPA news agency reported that the plane had transmitted an emergency code before landing, alerting air traffic control to a possible problem on board. "Checks at the scene established that there is no danger," police said in a statement. The nature of the alert was not immediately clear. Earlier in the morning, three pilots independently reported seeing an object that may have been a drone while taking off or landing at the airport. An onboard alert on a Corendon flight from Corfu prompted a temporary closure of Nuremberg airport Image: Daniel Löb/dpa/picture alliance Airport officials, border police and Germany's air traffic control service immediately launched a search involving a police helicopter, but no drone was found. Six flights were delayed, while two arriving aircraft diverted to Cologne and Prague before continuing to Nuremberg. It was initially unclear whether the two incidents were connected. Drone incidents disrupt German airports German airports have faced drone-related security alerts previously. In August, an explosives-laden drone was found near a runway at Leipzig/Halle airport , prompting a police investigation. Photograph: PR IMAGE View image in fullscreen Brendan Nugent has been named as the man arrested over the alleged vehicle attack on Indi MP Helen Haines in Wangaratta on Monday. Photograph: PR IMAGE Helen Haines Brendan Nugent’s family say Helen Haines has been their friend for more than 20 years Father of 43-year-old Tarrawingee man who allegedly attacked the independent MP says incident is ‘devastating and unfathomable’ Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria? Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Henry Belot and Nino Bucci Tue 20 Oct 2026 06.37 EDT First published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 21.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The father of a 43-year-old man accused of allegedly attacking Helen Haines has pledged to work with police and described the incident as “shocking and horrific”. The independent MP remained in a critical condition on Tuesday after being airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night. She has lost one leg, with surgeons working to save the other. Police confirmed a 43-year-old Tarrawingee man alleged to have driven the Toyota LandCruiser was arrested at the scene. Brendan Nugent was charged on Tuesday night with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the Commonwealth offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Victoria police confirmed in a statement that they would allege the attack was targeted. Nugent is expected to appear at Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday. ‘I don’t want to be known as a hero’: barber who rushed to help Helen Haines praised by PM Read more In a statement, Brendan Nugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and Rod’s partner, Christine Cunningham, said Haines had been their friend for more than 20 years. “What happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” they said. “We would like to sincerely thank members of the local community and police who came to Helen’s aid yesterday … We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community.” ‘Completely shocking’ Guardian Australia has spoken to local residents who have been concerned about Nugent’s behaviour for several years, including multiple allegations of abuse and threats from him. They reported erratic behaviour, shouting and music playing loudly until the early hours of the morning. They also raised concerns about his mental health. Nugent is a long-term forestry campaigner in the state’s north-east. Environment campaigners who worked with Nugent several years ago have expressed shock at his arrest. Nugent has a master’s of forest ecosystems science from the University of Melbourne and spent years researching the forestry industry in Victoria. He has also been a registered business owner in Wangaratta. Nugent was a committee member for the Save our Strathbogie Forest group, which campaigns against logging in the region. He became inactive around 2019-20. His arrest has shocked the group’s chair, Bertrant Lobert, who said he initially appeared to be “a reasonable and thoughtful person but then he drifted away”. “He was engaging, he was thoughtful and to hear what has happened now, if it all turns out to be true, is just completely shocking,” Lobert said. “This is quite personal as a lot of people in our group knew Helen personally and were friends. “This is more than just a tragedy about the targeting of public figures, it’s about our community and the people we know.” View image in fullscreen The scene of the alleged attack in Wangaratta. Photograph: Australian Broadcasting Corporation/Reuters Helen McKernan, the president of the Strathbogie Ranges Conservation Management Network Inc, also worked with Nugent as an activist before 2020. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion She says Nugent lost contact with her network of forestry campaigners around this date. “He was a committed activist,” McKernan said. “He would sleep out if necessary and help behind the scenes. We could always rely on him to turn up and contribute.” “It’s just a shock.” When the then-Victorian minister for environment, Lily D’Ambrosio, visited the Strathbogie forest in November 2019 to announce a ban on native forest logging, Nugent was among a group of about a dozen environmentalists who posed for photos. Also among the group was Rebecca Swift, a friend of Dezi Freeman who owned the property where he was living when two police officers were killed and a third injured in a shooting last year. Swift and Freeman shared conspiratorial beliefs about government and the Covid-19 pandemic, but it is unclear whether Nugent also embraced those views. “Lily I was so pleased to be in the Strathbogie forest to hear your announcement today,” Swift commented on D’Ambrosio’s Facebook post announcing the logging ban. “You gave us heart and hope that we are heard, and that our beloved wild landscapes are valued for so much more than merely dollars. Forest and wildlife defenders welcome a future where we can assist genuine governments to care for our national parks.” Swift was contacted for comment. The Victorian Nationals MP Tim McCurdy said Nugent was known to his Wangaratta office and regularly came in to raise different issues. “He’s been at our office,” McCurdy said. “We get plenty of people come in, half a dozen a day come for various things. So yes, he’s been into our office, [to raise] various issues. “Our office didn’t feel threatened by him, if they had they would ring the police. I want to wish Helen all the best.” In October 2019, when Nugent was still actively campaigning on forestry issues, he praised Haines for her stance on climate change.
